design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of beta-blocker use against no beta-blocker use in patients presenting with cocaine-associated chest pain. MEDLINE and EMBASE searched to 1 September 2016 with the terms 'beta blocker', 'cocaine' and six named beta blockers, plus hand-searching of reference lists of extracted studies and reviews, journal supplements, online highlights and direct discussion with experts; no language restriction. Eligible: retrospective or prospective studies in adults aged 18 or over with chest pain suspicious for acute coronary syndrome and cocaine use confirmed by a positive urine screen or self-report, comparing beta-blocker with no beta-blocker therapy and reporting non-fatal myocardial infarction or in-hospital all-cause mortality. 580 citations screened, five studies included, all retrospective and all from the USA, none randomized. Raw unadjusted event counts were pooled with Mantel-Haenszel random-effects odds ratios in Review Manager 5.1; heterogeneity by Cochran's Q and I-squared, with I-squared of 25% or more taken as significant; individual study quality rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; a funnel plot of the five studies was inspected for publication bias.
can_establish: What the five retrospective hospital cohorts published to September 2016 reported when their raw event counts are pooled: whether non-fatal myocardial infarction and death were more common among patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who were given a beta blocker, and how widely those cohorts disagree with one another.
cannot_establish: Whether beta blockers are safe in cocaine-associated chest pain. Every included study is a non-randomized comparison in which sicker patients were preferentially treated; the review pools unadjusted counts rather than the studies' own adjusted estimates, the myocardial-infarction analysis has I-squared of 71% with individual odds ratios running from 0.18 to 3.30, and the pooled confidence intervals (0.68 to 2.75 for infarction, 0.26 to 1.79 for death) exclude neither appreciable harm nor appreciable benefit. It also cannot establish anything about beta-blocker type, dose or route, which the authors state were not extractable, or about patients in whom cocaine was pharmacologically active, since exposure rests on urine screens that stay positive for days.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE and EMBASE to 1 September 2016 plus hand-searching and expert consultation; 580 citations screened to 5 included studies (pp. 2-3, Figure 1). All five are single- or two-centre retrospective US hospital studies published between 2008 and 2014, with inclusion periods from 1998 to 2011 (Table 1, p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: retrospective or prospective studies, adults aged 18 or over, chest pain suspicious for acute coronary syndrome as defined by each study, cocaine use by positive urine screen or self-report, and non-fatal myocardial infarction or in-hospital all-cause mortality reported, with a beta-blocker against no-beta-blocker comparison. Excluded: animal studies, case reports, observational studies, reviews, studies not focused on acute non-traumatic chest pain, studies without the outcomes of interest and studies without the comparison. No restriction by follow-up length or sample size (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Pooled across studies (Table 2, p. 3), no beta blocker against beta blocker: mean age 44.6 +/- 3.2 against 48.0 +/- 2.5 years (p < 0.001); male 67% against 71%; African-American 75% against 80% (p = 0.041); hypertension 40% against 97%; diabetes 15% against 26%; coronary artery disease 17% against 30%; hyperlipidaemia 10% against 20%; prior congestive heart failure 10% against 26% (all p < 0.001); lung disease 17% against 12% (p = 0.007); HIV 11% against 7% (p = 0.119); serum creatinine 1.5 +/- 0.2 against 1.8 +/- 0.4 mg/dl (p < 0.001). The denominators in this table are internally impossible in two rows (see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Attrition within the primary studies is not reported; three of the five studies contributed mortality data and all five contributed infarction data.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases with no registry or grey-literature search, no list of excluded studies, and a search closing 1 September 2016 for a paper published in June 2018, so about 21 months of literature is missing. All five included studies are retrospective US hospital cohorts, four of them single- or two-centre, from populations in which treatment was chosen by clinicians precisely on grounds that predict the outcome. The literature is small enough that a single study's extraction error or a single unpublished cohort could move the pooled estimate, and the funnel plot of five studies cannot detect that.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study recorded: administration of a beta blocker, in most of the included studies within the first 24 hours of presentation. Cocaine exposure by positive urine drug screen or reported use, as each study defined it. The review states that dose and route of the beta blocker were generally not delineated across studies and that outcomes by beta-blocker type (selective against non-selective) were not available, so neither could be analysed (p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable; not reported by the included studies in extractable form. Table 1 records the percentage of beta-1 selective agents in four of the five studies: 66%, not available, 87%, 61% and 47% (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level. The primary studies' handling of alcohol and other drug use is not extracted, and no study-level covariate for it appears.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Unknown and named as a limitation: urine toxicology can stay positive for 48 to 72 hours after use, so the timing and amount of cocaine cannot be established, although the authors argue urine testing reflects real-world practice and note that most included studies counted in-hospital events during a window in which cocaine might still interact with the drug given (p. 4).

comparison.controls: Within each primary study, patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who were not given a beta blocker.
comparison.matching: None at review level: raw 2 x 2 counts were pooled unadjusted, although several of the primary studies reported propensity-adjusted estimates of their own. The review does not say why unadjusted rather than adjusted estimates were combined.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Confounding by indication in every included study (the treated patients were older and had far more cardiovascular disease), co-prescribed anti-ischemic drugs, the timing of treatment relative to the outcome, and the amount, route and timing of cocaine use. None of these is adjusted for or explored at review level.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: All patients in both arms of every study were cocaine-positive; the contrast is between treatment decisions.

outcomes.instruments: As each primary study defined them. The infarction forest plot labels the outcome 'Myocardial Infarction (trop, EKG, symptoms)', that is troponin, electrocardiogram and symptoms, without a common threshold across studies (Figure 3, p. 4). Mortality is all-cause, stated in the eligibility criteria as in-hospital, although one included study contributed events over two years from presentation (pp. 2, 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, with up to 4 stars for selection, 2 for comparability and 3 for ascertainment of exposure and outcomes; 6 or more taken as high quality. All five studies scored 7 or 8 and were therefore all rated high quality (Table 1, p. 3), a result that does not separate them despite their estimates ranging from a fivefold apparent benefit to a threefold apparent harm.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Safety' is operationalized as the absence of a statistically significant pooled increase in non-fatal myocardial infarction or all-cause mortality.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: two pooled outcomes, no subgroup analyses and no meta-regression were performed, the authors stating that type-specific outcome data were unavailable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Study selection was done by two investigators reviewing abstracts, titles and full texts, and quality assessment and data extraction independently by three investigators (p. 2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mantel-Haenszel random-effects odds ratios. Non-fatal myocardial infarction, five studies, 94/610 (15.4%) with a beta blocker against 162/1146 (14.1%) without: pooled odds ratio 1.36 (95% CI 0.68 to 2.74 in Figure 3; the abstract and text give 0.68 to 2.75), Z = 0.87, p = 0.39, tau-squared 0.40, Q = 13.76 on 4 degrees of freedom (p = 0.008), I-squared 71%. The individual estimates run in both directions: Datillo 2008, 2/33 against 72/277, odds ratio 0.18 (0.04 to 0.79); Mohamad 2008, 14/100 against 13/264, 3.14 (1.42 to 6.95); Rangel 2010, 51/151 against 55/177, 1.13 (0.71 to 1.80); Ibrahim 2012, 22/162 against 20/216, 1.54 (0.81 to 2.93); Fanari 2014, 5/164 against 2/212, 3.30 (0.63 to 17.24). All-cause mortality, three studies, 6/348 (1.7%) against 22/666 (3.3%): pooled odds ratio 0.68 (0.26 to 1.79), Z = 0.79, p = 0.43, tau-squared 0.00, Q = 0.03 on 2 degrees of freedom (p = 0.98), I-squared 0%, from Datillo 1/33 against 13/277, 0.63 (0.08 to 5.01); Fanari 3/164 against 6/212, 0.64 (0.16 to 2.60); Rangel 2/151 against 3/177, 0.78 (0.13 to 4.72). No prediction interval, no absolute risk difference and no number needed to treat or harm is given. The Fanari counts in both analyses are percentages mistaken for counts (see reporting issues); recomputing them from the percentages Fanari prints gives odds ratios of about 2.67 for infarction and about 0.48 for death (editors' calculation from 8/164 against 4/212 and 5/164 against 13/212, the counts implied by Fanari's Table 3 percentages of 5%, 2%, 3% and 6%).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Unadjusted counts were pooled; the adjusted estimates several primary studies report were not used, and no meta-regression or subgroup analysis was attempted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, no registration number and no PROSPERO record are mentioned. The methods state the study was performed in compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses for Protocols statement, which is the guideline for writing protocols, while no protocol is reported (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Both prespecified outcomes are reported with forest plots and full counts, which is good practice. The narrative is where selection enters: the one study with a significant increase in infarction is described in the Results with the wrong citation and attributed to the study that in fact found a significant decrease, and the Discussion's statement that beta-blocker use has not been associated with worsening infarction cites the four studies including that one. Arrhythmia and stroke are mentioned as reported by three and two studies respectively, with the comment that no differences were noted, but no data for them are shown.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 256 infarction events and 28 deaths across the five studies leave intervals compatible with both substantial harm and substantial benefit; with I-squared of 71% in the infarction analysis the pooled interval understates the true dispersion, and no prediction interval is given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooling the raw counts of five retrospective US hospital cohorts, neither non-fatal myocardial infarction (odds ratio 1.36, 0.68 to 2.74) nor all-cause mortality (0.68, 0.26 to 1.79) differed significantly between patients given and not given a beta blocker. The infarction studies disagree sharply (I-squared 71%, tau-squared 0.40): one found a fivefold lower risk with a beta blocker and another a threefold higher risk, both statistically significant, with the remaining three in between. The mortality estimate is consistent across its three studies but rests on 28 deaths in total.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that beta-blocker use does not appear to be associated with an increased risk of infarction or mortality, and the discussion goes further: the results 'support contemporary clinical practice', suggest 'we reconsider the guidelines', and indicate that beta-blocker therapy 'may be a safe option' (pp. 1, 3). Four gaps. First, absence of evidence is read as evidence of absence: the infarction point estimate is 1.36, in the direction of harm, with an upper limit near 2.8. Second, a pooled estimate is presented as a summary of studies whose individual results point in opposite directions and are statistically incompatible; with I-squared of 71% the average is not a quantity that describes any of them. Third, the recommendation to reconsider guidelines rests entirely on non-randomized data in which the treated patients were systematically sicker, pooled without using the primary studies' own adjustment. Fourth, the review's narrative misstates its own forest plot about which study found harm. The limitations section is otherwise candid, naming the retrospective designs, the inability to date cocaine use, the absence of dose, route and drug-type data, the heterogeneity and the possibility of publication bias, and the conclusion calls for further study.

timeline.event: Intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow in cocaine-naive catheterization patients: the mechanistic basis of the guideline against beta blockers
Intravenous labetalol after intranasal cocaine lowered arterial pressure without relieving coronary vasoconstriction in the same laboratory
American Heart Association scientific statement advises against beta blockers in the acute setting, citing the catheterization studies
One of the five pooled cohorts: no detectable difference in in-hospital outcomes in 376 patients, with wide intervals
This meta-analysis pools the five retrospective cohorts and reports no significant difference in infarction or death

replication.where_it_stands: The review identifies the central fact of this literature: no randomized trial exists, and the guideline rests on two catheterization studies of 45 people in total conducted decades ago. What has accumulated since is retrospective hospital data that disagree with each other, and pooling them has not resolved the question. The Cocaine evidence list carries a second systematic review of the same five-or-so cohorts (Shin et al., 2019), published after this one and not appraised here; overlap between reviews of this small literature is near total and is not discussed in this paper, which describes itself as the first.

funding.funder: One author (Dr Addison) is supported by a K12-CA133250 grant; the remaining authors declare no specific grant for this research from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none declared. Patient consent not required. Provenance: not commissioned, externally peer reviewed (p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Johns Hopkins, Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard, Ohio State University, Baylor College of Medicine and the Michael E. DeBakey Veterans Affairs Medical Center. An interim analysis was presented at the American College of Cardiology Scientific Sessions in 2015, three years before publication (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of an intravenous beta blocker against the currently recommended alternatives in people presenting with chest pain after recent, confirmed cocaine use, powered for infarction and arrhythmia and with blinded outcome adjudication. Short of that, an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing cohorts, using each study's adjusted estimate, handling the timing of treatment relative to the event, and separating beta-1 selective agents from the combined alpha-beta blockers, would extract far more from this literature than pooling unadjusted counts does.

domains.domain: 1. Research questions and inclusion criteria include the components of PICO
domains.note: Population (adults with chest pain suspicious for acute coronary syndrome and cocaine use), intervention (beta blocker), comparator (no beta blocker) and outcomes (non-fatal myocardial infarction, in-hospital all-cause mortality) are all stated.

domains.domain: 2. Explicit statement that review methods were established before the review, and justification of deviations
domains.note: No protocol, registration or a priori statement. The methods cite compliance with the PRISMA statement for Protocols, which is the guideline for writing a protocol, while no protocol is reported anywhere.

domains.domain: 3. Explanation of the selection of study designs for inclusion
domains.note: The authors state they included retrospective or prospective studies because no randomized trials have been conducted. The same paragraph nevertheless lists 'observational studies' among the exclusions, which contradicts the five retrospective observational studies actually included.

Two databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE), keywords given, reference lists of included studies and reviews hand-searched, journal supplements and online highlights searched, experts consulted, no language restriction, search within 24 months of submission. Missing for a full yes: trial or study registries, an explicit grey-literature search and the full search strategy with limits.
Abstracts, titles and full-text articles were reviewed by two investigators.
Quality assessment and data extraction were independently performed by three investigators. The duplication did not catch the extraction error in the Fanari rows of both forest plots.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification for exclusions
domains.note: A flow diagram is given, but no list of the studies read in full and excluded, and no reasons for individual exclusions.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, setting, inclusion period, group sizes, percentage of beta-1 selective agents and quality score for each study. Missing: per-study populations, outcome definitions, follow-up windows and any dose or route detail, which the authors state was not available.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
domains.note: The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale covers selection, comparability (that is, confounding) and ascertainment of exposure and outcome, which meets the partial criterion for non-randomized studies, but not selection of the reported result. All five studies scored 7 or 8 of 9 and were classed as high quality despite confounding by indication being the dominant problem in each, so the instrument did not discriminate.

domains.domain: 10. Sources of funding of the included studies reported
domains.note: No funding information for any included study is reported.

Raw unadjusted counts from non-randomized studies were pooled with Mantel-Haenszel random effects, although several primary studies report propensity-adjusted estimates; no justification for combining unadjusted estimates is given, which is the specific requirement for non-randomized studies. Pooling proceeded despite I-squared of 71% on the primary outcome, above the review's own stated threshold of 25%.

domains.domain: 12. Assessment of the potential impact of risk of bias on the results of the meta-analysis
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis by study quality, by Newcastle-Ottawa score or by any design feature.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for when interpreting and discussing the results
domains.note: The limitations name the retrospective, non-randomized nature of the data and the resulting information and selection bias as the most prominent problem, though the conclusion that the therapy may be safe does not reflect it.

domains.domain: 14. Satisfactory explanation for, and discussion of, heterogeneity
domains.note: Heterogeneity is acknowledged and attributed in general terms to the non-randomized data, variable populations and few studies, but no subgroup analysis, meta-regression or outlier examination was performed, and the two studies with significant effects in opposite directions are not discussed as such.

domains.domain: 15. Adequate investigation of publication bias and discussion of its likely impact
domains.note: A funnel plot of five studies is presented and publication bias is named as a possible influence; a funnel plot with five studies cannot detect asymmetry and no statistical test was performed.

domains.domain: 16. Potential sources of conflict of interest, including funding for the review, reported
domains.note: Funding of one author stated and competing interests declared as none.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four of the seven critical items fail: no protocol (item 2), no list of excluded studies (item 7), inappropriate statistical combination (item 11) and no adequate assessment of publication bias (item 15), with item 9 only partially met. More than one critical weakness gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The review's own data, fully reported in the two forest plots, are its most useful product, and the limitations section is honest. The source can be cited for the fact that no randomized trial of beta blockers in cocaine-associated chest pain existed as of September 2016, for the identity and size of the five retrospective cohorts, and for their individual event counts and odds ratios as printed in Figures 3 and 4, with the caution that the Fanari rows are misextracted. It should not be cited for the pooled estimates as evidence that beta blockers are safe in this setting, and a claim resting on it must state the heterogeneity (I-squared 71%) and that one included study found a threefold increase in infarction.

key_findings.finding: Five retrospective US hospital studies published between 2008 and 2014, with inclusion periods from 1998 to 2011, met the criteria; no randomized trial of beta blockers in cocaine-associated chest pain was found. Newcastle-Ottawa scores were 7, 7, 8, 8 and 8 of 9.

Pooling all five studies, non-fatal myocardial infarction occurred in 94 of 610 patients (15.4%) given a beta blocker and 162 of 1146 (14.1%) not given one: random-effects odds ratio 1.36 (95% CI 0.68 to 2.74), Z = 0.87, p = 0.39, with tau-squared 0.40, Q = 13.76 on 4 degrees of freedom (p = 0.008) and I-squared 71%.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3, forest plot totals and heterogeneity line
key_findings.note: The abstract and the Results text give the upper confidence limit as 2.75 where the forest plot prints 2.74.

key_findings.finding: The five infarction estimates point in opposite directions: Datillo 2008 odds ratio 0.18 (0.04 to 0.79) from 2/33 against 72/277, Mohamad 2008 3.14 (1.42 to 6.95) from 14/100 against 13/264, Rangel 2010 1.13 (0.71 to 1.80), Ibrahim 2012 1.54 (0.81 to 2.93) and Fanari 2014 3.30 (0.63 to 17.24).
key_findings.note: Two of the five are individually significant and they disagree in direction: one shows roughly a fivefold lower risk with a beta blocker, the other a threefold higher risk. This is what the I-squared of 71% reflects.

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality, reported by three studies, occurred in 6 of 348 patients (1.7%) given a beta blocker and 22 of 666 (3.3%) not given one: odds ratio 0.68 (0.26 to 1.79), p = 0.43, tau-squared 0.00, Q = 0.03 on 2 degrees of freedom (p = 0.98), I-squared 0%.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4, forest plot totals and heterogeneity line
key_findings.note: 28 deaths in total across the three cohorts.

key_findings.finding: Patients given a beta blocker in the pooled baseline table were older (48.0 against 44.6 years) and had far more hypertension (97% against 40%), diabetes (26% against 15%), coronary artery disease (30% against 17%), hyperlipidaemia (20% against 10%) and prior heart failure (26% against 10%), while lung disease was more common in those not given one (17% against 12%).
key_findings.note: Two rows of this table are internally impossible (see reporting issues), so the pooled percentages should be treated as indicative only.

key_findings.finding: The review states that beta-blocker dose and route were generally not delineated across the included studies, that overlap or switching of agents could not be excluded, and that outcomes by beta-blocker type (selective against non-selective) were not available, so no analysis by drug class was possible.
key_findings.note: This is the specific gap that keeps the review from testing the mechanism it is about, since the concern applies to unopposed beta-blockade rather than to agents that also block alpha receptors.

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the guideline recommendations against beta blockers here derive from animal studies, expert opinion and two haemodynamic studies of 45 human participants in total, given intravenous beta blockers in a catheterization laboratory nearly three decades earlier.
key_findings.note: The two studies cited are Lange et al. 1990 and Boehrer et al. 1993, which together enrolled 45 patients (30 and 15).

key_findings.finding: The authors name as limitations the retrospective non-randomized data with information and selection bias, urine screens staying positive for 48 to 72 hours so that timing and amount of cocaine cannot be established, the inability to exclude that some patients were given beta blockers for haemodynamic reasons rather than chest pain, the significant heterogeneity, and possible publication bias and lack of access to primary patient data.

The authors conclude that beta-blocker therapy may be a safe option in patients presenting with chest pain and suspected cocaine use, that the results support contemporary clinical practice, and that the guidelines on beta blockers in this setting should be reconsidered.
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' interpretation; the pooled infarction point estimate is 1.36 with an upper confidence limit near 2.8, and the analysis is of unadjusted counts from non-randomized studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fanari rows of both forest plots appear to be the percentages printed in that study's Table 3 entered as event counts. Figure 3 gives Fanari 5/164 against 2/212 and Figure 4 gives 3/164 against 6/212, which are exactly the numbers 5, 2, 3 and 6 that Fanari prints as percentages under a column headed 'BB (%)'. The counts those percentages imply are about 8 and 4 for infarction and about 5 and 13 for death.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both of Fanari's contributions are wrong, in opposite directions. Recomputed from the percentages, its infarction odds ratio is about 2.67 rather than 3.30 and its mortality odds ratio about 0.48 rather than 0.64 (editors' calculation). Fanari carried 11.4% of the infarction analysis but 48.5% of the mortality analysis, so the pooled mortality estimate is the one materially affected. Exact counts cannot be recovered, because the source prints only rounded percentages; a claim citing the pooled mortality estimate should say so.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that one early study showed a statistically significant increase in myocardial infarction with beta-blocker use and cite reference 15 (Datillo et al.), whose entry in Figure 3 is an odds ratio of 0.18 (0.04 to 0.79), a significant decrease, and whose own title reports beta blockers as associated with reduced risk. The study that showed a significant increase is Mohamad et al. (reference 16), odds ratio 3.14 (1.42 to 6.95).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence that acknowledges harm in the included literature points at the wrong study. Compounding this, the Discussion states that beta-blocker use has not been associated with worsening non-fatal infarction and cites references 16 to 19, a list that includes the very study with the significant threefold increase. A reader relying on the narrative rather than the forest plot would conclude that no included study found harm.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 reports 365 patients with hypertension among 348 assessed in the beta-blocker group (97%), a count larger than its own denominator, and gives the number assessed for mean age as 1157 in the no-beta-blocker group and 637 in the beta-blocker group, both larger than the group totals of 1146 and 610 stated in the same table heading.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least three numbers in the baseline table are impossible, so the pooled baseline comparison cannot be verified. Since the imbalance in this table is the review's evidence that the treated patients were sicker, the direction of the argument survives but its magnitudes should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants is given as 1794 in the abstract and in the first line of the discussion, and as 1756 in the Results and in both forest plots; the study-level totals in Table 1 sum to 1756 (1146 plus 610).
reporting_issues.consequence: A 38-patient discrepancy with no explanation. Claims should use 1756, which matches the analysed data.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility paragraph lists 'observational studies' among the exclusions while the inclusion criterion admits retrospective or prospective studies, and all five included studies are retrospective observational cohorts.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated design criterion is self-contradictory, so the reader cannot tell what was eligible; in practice the review included exactly the design its exclusion list rules out.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility criteria specify all-cause mortality in hospital, but the review states that one included study (Rangel et al.) contributed events over two years from presentation, and the paper does not say whether the in-hospital or the two-year mortality figure was pooled.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mortality analysis may mix follow-up windows differing by two orders of magnitude in duration, which would make the pooled odds ratio uninterpretable as a rate. Which estimate entered Figure 4 cannot be determined from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state compliance with the PRISMA statement for Protocols, a guideline for writing review protocols, while no protocol, registration number or a priori analysis plan is reported; the relevant reporting guideline for a completed review is PRISMA itself.
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation gives an impression of prospective planning that the paper does not support. The review should be read as unregistered.

reporting_issues.issue: The review defines I-squared of 25% or more as significant heterogeneity, finds 71% in the primary analysis, and proceeds to pool and to recommend reconsidering guidelines, with the explanation that guidance was needed; no prediction interval, subgroup analysis or meta-regression accompanies the pooled estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled odds ratio of 1.36 summarises studies that are statistically incompatible with one another. Any claim citing it must carry the heterogeneity, and the individual study estimates are more informative than the average.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 dates Ibrahim et al. to 2012 while the reference list gives 2013, and the same study's name is spelled Datillo in Table 1 and the figures but Dattilo in the reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor bibliographic inconsistency; it matters only for matching the included studies to their records.
